segment.text: 近年にない暑さである。どこを見ても、泥で固めた家々の屋根瓦が、鉛のやうに鈍く日の光を反射して、その下に懸けてある燕の巣さへ、この塩梅では中にゐる雛や卵を、そのまゝ蒸殺してしまふかと思はれる。まして、畑と云ふ畑は、麻でも黍でも、皆、土いきれにぐつたりと頭をさげて、何一つ、青いなりに、萎れてゐないものはない。その畑の上に見える空も、この頃の温気に中てられたせいか、地上に近い大気は、晴れながら、どんよりと濁つて、その所々に、霰を炮烙で煎つたやうな、形ばかりの雲の峰が、つぶつぶと浮かんでゐる。――「酒虫」の話は、この陽気に、わざ〳〵炎天の打麦場へ出てゐる、三人の男で始まるのである。

sentences.text: 近年にない暑さである。
どこを見ても、泥で固めた家々の屋根瓦が、鉛のやうに鈍く日の光を反射して、その下に懸けてある燕の巣さへ、この塩梅では中にゐる雛や卵を、そのまゝ蒸殺してしまふかと思はれる。
まして、畑と云ふ畑は、麻でも黍でも、皆、土いきれにぐつたりと頭をさげて、何一つ、青いなりに、萎れてゐないものはない。
その畑の上に見える空も、この頃の温気に中てられたせいか、地上に近い大気は、晴れながら、どんよりと濁つて、その所々に、霰を炮烙で煎つたやうな、形ばかりの雲の峰が、つぶつぶと浮かんでゐる。
――「酒虫」の話は、この陽気に、わざ〳〵炎天の打麦場へ出てゐる、三人の男で始まるのである。

segment.text: 不思議な事に、その中の一人は、素裸で、仰向けに地面へ寝ころんでゐる。おまけに、どう云ふ訳だか、細引で、手も足もぐる〳〵巻にされてゐる。が格別当人は、それを苦に病んでゐる容子もない。背の低い、血色の好い、どことなく鈍重と云ふ感じを起させる、豚のやうに肥つた男である。それから手ごろな素焼の瓶が一つ、この男の枕もとに置いてあるが、これも中に何がはいつてゐるのだか、わからない。

segment.text: もう一人は、黄色い法衣を着て、耳に小さな青銅の環をさげた、一見、象貌の奇古な沙門である。皮膚の色が並はづれて黒い上に、髪や鬚の縮れてゐる所を見ると、どうも葱嶺の西からでも来た人間らしい。これはさつきから根気よく、朱柄の麈尾をふりふり、裸の男にたからうとする虻や蠅を追つてゐたが、流石に少しくたびれたと見えて、今では、例の素焼の瓶の側へ来て、七面鳥のやうな恰好をしながら、勿体らしくしやがんでゐる。

sentences.text: もう一人は、黄色い法衣を着て、耳に小さな青銅の環をさげた、一見、象貌の奇古な沙門である。
皮膚の色が並はづれて黒い上に、髪や鬚の縮れてゐる所を見ると、どうも葱嶺の西からでも来た人間らしい。
これはさつきから根気よく、朱柄の麈尾をふりふり、裸の男にたからうとする虻や蠅を追つてゐたが、流石に少しくたびれたと見えて、今では、例の素焼の瓶の側へ来て、七面鳥のやうな恰好をしながら、勿体らしくしやがんでゐる。

segment.text: あとの一人は、この二人からずつと離れて、打麦場の隅にある草房の軒下に立つてゐる。この男は、頤の先に、鼠の尻尾のやうな髯を、申訳だけに生やして、踵が隠れる程長い皁布衫に、結目をだらしなく垂らした茶褐帯と云ふ拵へである。白い鳥の羽で製つた団扇を、時々大事さうに使つてゐる容子では、多分、儒者か何かにちがひない。
segment.source: あとの一人は、この二人からずつと離れて、打麦場の隅にある草房の軒下に立つてゐる。この男は、頤《あご》の先に、鼠の尻尾のやうな髯《ひげ》を、申訳だけに生やして、踵が隠れる程長い※［＃「白／十」、第3水準1-88-64］布衫《さうふさん》に、結目をだらしなく垂らした茶褐帯《さかつたい》と云ふ拵へである。白い鳥の羽で製《つく》つた団扇を、時々大事さうに使つてゐる容子では、多分、儒者か何かにちがひない。

sentences.text: 日は正に、亭午であらう。
犬も午睡をしてゐるせいか、吠える声一つ聞えない。
打麦場を囲んでゐる麻や黍も、青い葉を日に光らせて、ひつそりかんと静まつてゐる。
それから、その末に見える空も、一面に、熱くるしく、炎靄をたゞよはせて、雲の峰さへもこの旱に、肩息をついてゐるのかと、疑はれる。
見渡した所、息が通つてゐるらしいのは、この三人の男の外にない。
さうして、その三人が又、関帝廟に安置してある、泥塑の像のやうに沈黙を守つてゐる。

segment.text: 裸で、炎天に寝ころんでゐるのは、この打麦場の主人で、姓は劉、名は大成と云ふ、長山では、屈指の素封家の一人である。この男の道楽は、酒を飲む一方で、朝から、殆、盃を離したと云ふ事がない。それも、「独酌する毎に輒、一甕を尽す」と云ふのだから、人並をはづれた酒量である。尤も前にも云つたやうに、「負郭の田三百畝、半は黍を種う」と云ふので、飲の為に家産が累はされるやうな惧は、万々ない。

それも、「独酌する毎に輒、一甕を尽す」と云ふのだから、人並をはづれた酒量である。
尤も前にも云つたやうに、「負郭の田三百畝、半は黍を種う」と云ふので、飲の為に家産が累はされるやうな惧は、万々ない。

segment.text: それが、何故、裸で、炎天に寝ころんでゐるかと云ふと、それには、かう云ふ因縁がある。――その日、劉が、同じ飲仲間の孫先生と一しよに（これが、白羽扇を持つてゐた儒者である。）風通しのいゝ室で、竹婦人に靠れながら、棋局を闘はせてゐると、召使ひの丫鬟が来て、「唯今、宝幢寺とかにゐると云ふ、坊さんが御見えになりまして、是非、御主人に御目にかゝりたいと申しますが、いかゞ致しませう。」と云ふ。

segment.text: 「なに、宝幢寺？」かう云つて、劉は小さな眼を、まぶしさうに、しばたたいたが、やがて、暑さうに肥つた体を起しながら、「では、こゝへ御通し申せ。」と云ひつけた。それから、孫先生の顔をちよいと見て「大方あの坊主でせう。」とつけ加へた。

segment.text: 宝幢寺にゐる坊主と云ふのは、西域から来た蛮僧である。これが、医療も加へれば、房術も施すと云ふので、この界隈では、評判が高い。たとへば、張三の黒内障が、忽、快方に向つたとか、李四の病閹が、即座に平癒したとか、殆、奇蹟に近い噂が盛に行はれてゐるのである。――この噂は、二人とも聞いてゐた。その蛮僧が、今、何の用で、わざわざ、劉の所へ出むいて来たのであらう。勿論、劉の方から、迎へにやつた覚えなどは、全然ない。

segment.text: 序に云つて置くが、劉は、一体、来客を悦ぶやうな男ではない。が、他に一人、来客がある場合に、新来の客が来たとなると、大抵ならば、快く会つてやる。客の手前、客のあるのを自慢するとでも云つたらよささうな、小供らしい虚栄心を持つてゐるからである。それに、今日の蛮僧は、この頃、どこででも評判になつてゐる。決して、会つて恥しいやうな客ではない。――劉が会はうと云ひ出した動機は、大体こんな所にあつたのである。

segment.text: こんな事を、二人で話してゐる内に、やがて、丫鬟の案内で、はいつて来たのを見ると、背の高い、紫石稜のやうな眼をした、異形な沙門である。黄色い法衣を着て、その肩に、縮れた髪の伸びたのを、うるささうに垂らしてゐる。それが、朱柄の麈尾を持つたまゝ、のつそり室のまん中に立つた。挨拶もしなければ、口もきかない。

segment.text: 孫先生は、元来、道仏の二教を殆、無理由に軽蔑してゐる。だから、道士とか僧侶とかと一しよになつても、口をきいた事は滅多にない。それが、今ふと口を出す気になつたのは、全く酒虫と云ふ語の興味に動かされたからで、酒の好きな先生は、これを聞くと、自分の腹の中にも、酒虫がゐはしないかと、聊、不安になつて来たのである。所が、蛮僧の不承不承な答を聞くと、急に、自分が莫迦にされたやうな気がしたので、先生はちよいと顔をしかめながら、又元の通り、黙々として棋子を下しはじめた。さうして、それと同時に、内心、こんな横柄な坊主に会つたり何ぞする主人の劉を、莫迦げてゐると思ひ出した。

だから、道士とか僧侶とかと一しよになつても、口をきいた事は滅多にない。
それが、今ふと口を出す気になつたのは、全く酒虫と云ふ語の興味に動かされたからで、酒の好きな先生は、これを聞くと、自分の腹の中にも、酒虫がゐはしないかと、聊、不安になつて来たのである。

sentences.text: 酒虫と云ふ物が、どんな物だか、それが腹の中にゐなくなると、どうなるのだか、枕もとにある酒の瓶は、何にするつもりなのだか、それを知つてゐるのは、蛮僧の外に一人もない。
かう云ふと、何も知らずに、炎天へ裸で出てゐる劉は、甚、迂濶なやうに思はれるが、普通の人間が、学校の教育などをうけるのも、実は大抵、これと同じやうな事をしてゐるのである。

segment.text: 暑い。額へ汗がぢりぢりと湧いて来て、それが玉になつたかと思ふと、つうつと生暖く、眼の方へ流れて来る。生憎、細引でしばられてゐるから、手を出して拭ふ訳には、勿論行かない。そこで、首を動かして、汗の進路を変へやうとすると、その途端に、はげしく眩暈がしさうな気がしたので、残念ながら、この計画も亦、見合せる事にした。その中に、汗は遠慮なく、眶をぬらして、鼻の側から口許をまはりながら、頤の下まで流れて行く。気味が悪い事夥しい。

sentences.text: 暑い。
額へ汗がぢりぢりと湧いて来て、それが玉になつたかと思ふと、つうつと生暖く、眼の方へ流れて来る。
生憎、細引でしばられてゐるから、手を出して拭ふ訳には、勿論行かない。
そこで、首を動かして、汗の進路を変へやうとすると、その途端に、はげしく眩暈がしさうな気がしたので、残念ながら、この計画も亦、見合せる事にした。
その中に、汗は遠慮なく、眶をぬらして、鼻の側から口許をまはりながら、頤の下まで流れて行く。
気味が悪い事夥しい。

segment.text: それまでは、眼を開いて、白く焦された空や、葉をたらした麻畑を、まじ〳〵と眺めてゐたが、汗が無暗に流れるやうになつてからは、それさへ断念しなければならなくなつた。劉は、この時、始めて、汗が眼にはいると、しみるものだと云ふ事を、知つたのである。そこで、屠所の羊の様な顔をして、神妙に眼をつぶりながら、ぢつと日に照りつけられてゐると、今度は、顔と云はず体と云はず、上になつてゐる部分の皮膚が、次第に或痛みを感じるやうになつて来た。皮膚の全面に、あらゆる方向へ動かうとする力が働いてゐるが、皮膚自身は、それに対して、毫も弾力を持つてゐない。それでどこもかしこも、ぴり〳〵する――とでも説明したら、よからうと思ふ痛みである。これは、汗所の苦しさではない。劉は、少し蛮僧の治療をうけたのが、忌々しくなつて来た。

そこで、屠所の羊の様な顔をして、神妙に眼をつぶりながら、ぢつと日に照りつけられてゐると、今度は、顔と云はず体と云はず、上になつてゐる部分の皮膚が、次第に或痛みを感じるやうになつて来た。

これは、汗所の苦しさではない。
劉は、少し蛮僧の治療をうけたのが、忌々しくなつて来た。

segment.text: しかし、これは、後になつて考へて見ると、まだ苦しくない方の部だつたのである。――そのうちに、喉が渇いて来た。劉も、曹孟徳か誰かが、前路に梅林ありと云つて、軍士の渇を医したと云ふ事は知つてゐる。が、今の場合、いくら、梅子の甘酸を念頭に浮べて見ても、喉の渇く事は、少しも前と変りがない。頤を動かして見たり、舌を噛んで見たりしたが、口の中は依然として熱を持つてゐる。それも、枕もとの素焼の瓶がなかつたら、まだ幾分でも、我慢がし易かつたのに違ひない。所が、瓶の口からは、芬々たる酒香が、間断なく、劉の鼻を襲つて来る。しかも、気のせいか、その酒香が、一分毎に、益々高くなつて来るやうな心もちさへする。劉は、せめて、瓶だけでも見ようと思つて、眼をあけた。上眼を使つて見ると、瓶の口と、応揚にふくれた胴の半分ばかりが、眼にはいる。眼にはいるのは、それだけであるが、同時に、劉の想像には、その瓶のうす暗い内部に、黄金のやうな色をした酒のなみ〳〵と湛へてゐる容子が、浮んで来た。思はず、ひびの出来た唇を、乾いた舌で舐めまはして見たが、唾の湧く気色は、更にない。汗さへ今では、日に干されて、前のやうには、流れなくなつてしまつた。

segment.text: 蛮僧の治療の効は、覿面に現れた。劉大成は、その日から、ぱつたり酒が飲めなくなつたのである。今は、匂を嗅ぐのも、嫌だと云ふ。所が、不思議な事に、劉の健康が、それから、少しづつ、衰へて来た。今年で、酒虫を吐いてから、三年になるが、往年の丸丸と肥つてゐた俤は、何処にもない。色光沢の悪い皮膚が、脂じみたまま、険しい顔の骨を包んで、霜に侵された双髩が、纔に、顳顬の上に、残つてゐるばかり、一年の中に、何度、床につくか、わからない位ださうである。

そこで、もし酒虫を除かなかつたなら、劉は必久しからずして、死んだのに相違ない。
して見ると、貧病、迭に至るのも、寧劉にとつては、幸福と云ふべきである。

chapter_summaries.0: Part I. Blazing heat over tiled roofs, fields, cloud-peaks. Three men on Liu threshing-floor at noon: one naked, bound hand and foot, with unglazed jar at pillow; one dark-skinned western monk in yellow robe with fly-whisk; one long-gowned man with white-feather fan under eaves. All silent, barely moving, like clay statues in a Guandi temple. Narrator adds: not Japan but Changshan, China.

hard_spots.why_hard: 「独酌する毎に輒、一甕を尽す」 and 「負郭の田三百畝、半は黍を種う」 are quoted as proof-texts for prodigious drinking and wealth. Need to keep as quotations, not naturalise, and keep mu as mu with note; rendering jar/cask must match the jar at the pillow.
comparison of Liu's ignorant submission to schooling is cool authorial irony, not compassion; ennobling it into satire on education or softening it misplaces tone.
Cao Mengde's plum grove to cure thirst; Liu tries the trick and it fails. Needs minimal note only; context already gives sense.

expulsion similes shift earthworm / gecko / loach, then jar animal: flesh-red like red clay, like small salamander, three sun long, with mouth and eyes, apparently drinking as it swims. Must not reduce to bug or parasite and must keep shifting likeness, not fix one animal.

three answers must stay evenly weighted and aphoristic, especially third: Liu is the worm, the worm is Liu. Buddhist colour and plain identity at once; must not sound like quoted Zen wisdom nor like explanation.

narrator confesses ignorance and says he imitates the Didacticism of Chinese novelists, capital D in source, then signs 五年四月. Keep capitalised foreign word and dry sign-off; do not turn into wise closure. Date is ambiguous year-month; annotate, do not resolve.

motifs.english: always wine worm as two-word creature, never bug, parasite, or worm alone where source says wine worm
motifs.why: title and diagnosis; varying it breaks the case-history link from gossip to jar to moral debate.

motifs.english: keep wine, to drink, to be drunk, drinking as one family; do not vary to liquor, booze, tipple
motifs.why: prodigious drinking without drunkenness is the symptom; loss even of smell is the cure's mark; variation would hide identity claim in third answer.

motifs.english: keep heat vocabulary linked: heat, blazing sun, noon, dry spell, haze; same dry glare from tableau to torture
motifs.why: weather of Part I becomes bodily torment of Part III; thinning it breaks deliberate return.

motifs.english: keep silence and stillness flat: shut mouths, barely move, do not stir, quiet; statues comparison once
motifs.why: tableau is defined by withheld speech and movement, mirrored in required stillness of cure; explanatory connectives would rationalise it away.

motifs.english: always unglazed earthen jar; introduce as unexplained object, identify contents only when narrator does
motifs.motif: the unglazed jar at the pillow
motifs.why: planted as mystery in Part I, explained as lure in Part II, heard then seen in Part III; naming contents early destroys structure.

motifs.english: keep smell growing minute by minute; fragrance assailing nose without break
motifs.why: thirst-torture turns on smell, and loss even of smelling marks cure; keep verbal link, not varied perfume/aroma.

narration.english_tense: past as default for reported action; keep present where Japanese uses non-past for tableau and bodily sensation (p2 heat tableau, p44-p46 sweat, thirst, prickling), so weather and torture stay immediate and linked. Do not backshift those presents into past.
narration.frame: faux-scholarly retelling of a Chinese anecdote: unexplained noon tableau, break to locate as Changshan China not Japan, slow flashback with deferrals and self-cross-reference, single-body present-tense cure, three-year jump, enumerated morals declined, dated sign-off.
narration.narrator: first-person only at close as 自分; otherwise third-person intermediary who cites, quotes, digresses and poses as imitator of Chinese novelists. Learned and sensuous, coolly ironic, never on reader's side.
narration.tense_habits: Japanese mixes である / ている tableaux and commentary with た action and present-tense sensation (暑い, 流れる, 感じる). Shifts mark the four movements, not errors.
timeline: one summer noon: tableau on Liu threshing-floor (Part I)
same day earlier: chess, visit, consent, binding (Part II flashback)
same noon continued: sweating, thirst, expulsion into jar (Part III)
three years later: Liu sick, poor, unrecognisable; debate in Changshan; narrator lists three answers, confesses ignorance (Part IV)

part_summaries.summary: Part I. Blazing heat over tiled roofs, fields, cloud-peaks. Three men on Liu threshing-floor at noon: one naked, bound hand and foot, with unglazed jar at pillow; one dark-skinned western monk in yellow robe with fly-whisk; one long-gowned man with white-feather fan under eaves. All silent, barely moving, like clay statues in a Guandi temple. Narrator adds: not Japan but Changshan, China.

Part II. The naked man is owner Liu Dacheng, rich in 300 mu, who drinks a jar at a sitting and never gets drunk. Playing chess with drinking friend Sun Sensei, he admits the famed western monk from Hodoji temple. Monk without greeting diagnoses a wine worm in belly as cause of never drunkenness and offers cure by lying naked still in sun. Sun asks once about drugs, is rebuffed, falls silent. Liu consents from ease, curiosity and vanity; is bound with cord, jar of wine set at pillow, Sun stays to watch.

Part III. Liu alone in heat: sweat into eyes he cannot wipe, dizziness, skin prickling as if pulled all ways, raging thirst sharpened by unbroken smell of wine from jar, headache. As he opens mouth to stop cure, a soft mass crawls up gullet like earthworm, like gecko, slips out like loach with a plop into jar. Monk unties him: worm is out. All three peer in: flesh-red like red clay, like small salamander about three sun long, with mouth and eyes, seemingly drinking as it swims. Liu feels sick.

Part IV. Cure works at once: Liu cannot drink, cannot bear smell. In three years health fails, former fat figure gone, often bedridden; 300 mu mostly lost, he ploughs himself. Narrator poses why health and estate failed and lists three representative answers from Changshan people: worm was fortune lost through folly; worm was disease and poverty is better than death; worm was neither because Liu was the worm. Declares he does not know which is right, has only listed them in imitation of Chinese novelists' Didacticism. Signs Fifth year, fourth month.

body.say: Cure works and ruins; text refuses to choose among fortune, disease, or identity readings. Keep tableau unexplained, monk rude and unexplained, dialogue flat against elaborate heat-writing, worm concrete with mouth and eyes, three answers parallel and declined, sign-off dry.

style_sheet.annotation_density: sparse; note only what sentence cannot give: mu, sun, Baodong/Hodoji temple name form, Cao Mengde plum-grove trick, Guandi temple statues, Didacticism capitalisation. Never gloss worm, method, or morals.
style_sheet.author_voice: learned and sensuous at once: dense Sino-Japanese heat similes and bodily accumulation in plain sequence, short flat dialogue, dry ironic asides and self-references. English should squirm in Part III, not shudder in gothic; should enumerate in Part IV, not elegise.
style_sheet.honorifics_and_names: Chinese pinyin for Chinese places and persons to keep not-Japan frame explicit: Liu Dacheng, Changshan, Zhang San, Li Si, Cao Mengde; temple as Hodoji (Baodong) with note on Japanese reading versus Chinese Baochuang. Keep Sun Sensei with Sensei, not Master Sun or Mr Sun, because text prints 孫先生 with Japanese ruby and Japanese mediation is part of pose; narrator's 自分 as I with no honorific inflation.
style_sheet.keep_in_japanese: keep Didacticism exactly capitalised as in source; keep mu for 田 measure and sun for worm length with note; keep shubi, yahuan, Guandi on first use with gloss if needed, then plain English; do not keep ordinary words in Japanese.
style_sheet.quotation: Japanese 「」 and 『』 to English double quotes; keep quoted set Chinese phrases as quotations to show pose of citation.
style_sheet.register: slightly formal, faintly archaic learned English for narration; plain contemporary for dialogue, especially monk's bluntness. No picturesque exoticism, no modern slang, no moralising adjectives that favour one answer.
style_sheet.ruby_and_italics: no ruby in English; do not reproduce glosses like つばめ except in notes if needed. Italics only for romanised terms kept in Japanese and for the printed English word Didacticism, matching source emphasis.

fork.question: Whether two readers have named the same crux or different cruxes

head.reason: Both options name the same crux in different words: a cure that must remain undecidably ruinous, held in three equally weighted closing answers, and a faux-scholarly, detached Chinese-tale voice whose distance makes the one passage of bodily torment work. Option 1 states that twin crux most cleanly, with its evidence tied to the text and without turning either reader's useful directing details into a second, competing crux.
head.say: House log: The two independent readings were judged to name the same crux, and Option 1 was picked as the wording to go forward.

crux.for_the_english: Keep all three explanations syntactically parallel, equally weighted and in the same dry register, and keep the narrator's refusal to judge — and his borrowed word 'Didacticism' — flat and ironic. Do not let vocabulary tilt the scale: the monk must not become a charlatan or a fool in the telling, Liu not a drunkard reformed or a victim, the worm not 'parasite' (clinical), 'demon' (supernatural) or 'gift' (allegorical) by default. Where a word must lean, the margin should say so.
crux.point: The story stands or falls on the cure being indistinguishable from the ruin — the worm must remain literally a worm and undecidably disease, fortune, and Liu himself, to the last line.
crux.why: Expelling the creature works exactly as promised: from that day Liu cannot drink, cannot even bear the smell (p53). Yet health and the three hundred mu of fields go with the drinking (p53–54), and the narrator closes not with a moral but with three incompatible answers — worm as heaven-given fortune lost through a benighted monk; worm as disease whose removal, even into poverty and sickness, is still happiness; worm as neither, because 'Liu is the wine worm, the wine worm is Liu,' so removing it was a kind of self-killing (p56–58) — followed by an explicit refusal to choose: 'which of these answers is most apt, I myself do not know' (p59). Earlier details are planted to serve all three readings at once: the drinking that never makes him drunk (p26–27), the wealth that makes the drinking costless (p10), a whole life with nothing in it but wine (p58).

crux.for_the_english: Hold a slightly formal, old-tale surface — kept terms, quoted sayings, unhurried periodic sentences — without fake archaism or orientalist quaintness, and do not smooth the gear-change into section three: let the detached chronicle give way to present, physical, almost clinical suffering and then back again. Foreign terms should stay strange where the Japanese keeps them strange, glossed in the margin rather than domesticated in the line.
crux.point: The voice is a pastiche — a modern author performing a Chinese strange tale — and its dry, learned detachment against one prolonged passage of bodily torment is the story's engine, not decoration.
crux.why: The narration wears its borrowed costume openly: a Chinese setting announced as an afterthought ('Of course, this is not a story of Japan,' p8), Sino-learned diction and set phrases ('at every solitary drinking he would finish a whole jar,' p10), storyteller's asides to the reader (p42, comparing Liu's ignorance to anyone who receives an education), statuesque tableaux in the opening heat (p2–7), and a closing bow to 'the Didacticism of Chinese novelists' (p59). Against that cool frame, section three drops into Liu's skin — sweat stinging his eyes, skin prickling without elasticity, thirst fixed on the smell from the jar at his pillow, the thing crawling up his gullet like earthworm, gecko, loach (p44–48) — rendered slowly and without euphemism. Flatten either side and the tale becomes either a quaint anecdote or a horror vignette; the irony lives in the distance between them.

second.say: The crux (one or two items), each with its reason and what follows for the English; a line on how confident you are and what would change your mind. Keep it under a page.
second.what_would_change_my_mind: Evidence that Akutagawa is translating or closely adapting a specific Chinese source whose own wording settles the worm's status or dictates the register — then fidelity to that source's choices, rather than to the ambiguity, would govern.

body.why: The book's four brief numbered sections make one continuous short story well under the length limit, so joining them preserves the voice and arc for a single reading.

crux.for_the_english: Give the sensation in plain present-tense accumulation, not gothic description. The English should squirm, not shudder.
crux.point: A man is cured of the thing that made him himself, and the story will not say whether the cure saved or killed him.
crux.why: Liu Dacheng drinks a cask at a sitting and never gets drunk. A rude monk from the west says a wine worm lives in his belly, ties him naked in the noon heat of his own threshing-floor with a jar of wine at his pillow, and the worm, lured by the smell, crawls up his throat and drops into the jar — a three-inch, flesh-red, salamander-like thing with mouth and eyes, apparently drinking as it swims. From that day Liu cannot bear even the smell of wine. Within three years his health, then his three hundred mu of fields, then his whole former self are gone. Part IV then stops the story and lines up three answers — the worm was his fortune, not his disease; the worm was his disease, and poverty and sickness are still better than the death it would have brought; the worm was neither, because Liu was the worm and in losing it he killed himself — and the narrator says he does not know which is right, and that he has only listed them in imitation of the Didacticism of Chinese novelists. Every earlier pleasure of the tale, the heat, the grotesque cure, the comedy of the three waiting men, is retroactively put in question by that refusal. If the English lets any one answer win — by a sympathetic adjective for Liu, a sinister one for the monk, a wry or a mournful colouring in the final paragraphs — it has decided a case the text leaves open and become a fable about alcohol, or about quacks, or about genius destroyed by normality. None of those is this story.

crux.for_the_english: Keep the three answers parallel, evenly weighted and evenly plausible, in the same enumerating syntax. Keep the monk rude, abrupt and unexplained from first to last: he gives no greeting, answers Sun's questions ungraciously, states his diagnosis as fact. Do not make him a sage, a charlatan or a tempter. Keep Liu neither fool nor victim in the diction: he consents out of vanity, curiosity and a childish wish to show off a famous visitor, and the narrator reports those motives as coolly as he reports the weather.
crux.point: The narrator is a faux-scholarly intermediary, not a storyteller on the reader's side, and his asides are part of the mechanism.
crux.why: The tale is framed as a Chinese anecdote retold: it opens on the threshing-floor tableau with no explanation, breaks off to say of course this is not Japan but an incident at Changshan in China, flashes back with repeated deferrals ('the reason he lies there is this'), cross-refers to itself ('as said before'), quotes drinking and acreage in set Chinese phrases, digresses to compare Liu's ignorant submission to the treatment with ordinary people submitting to schooling, and signs off with a date. The erudition is real and also a pose; the citations and the numbered moral answers mimic a Chinese source the reader cannot check. That distance is what lets the impossible worm be reported like a case history.

open_questions.question: How far to reproduce the pose of scholarship in English: keep the capitalised foreign word 'Didacticism' as Akutagawa prints it, keep the quoted set phrases as quotations, and keep the self-references ('as said before') — or naturalise any of them? Naturalising is smoother and loses the frame.
open_questions.why_it_matters: These are the visible seams of the retelling. Cut or soften them and the story reads as an original fable; keep them stiffly and it reads as pastiche. The choice governs the whole register.

open_questions.question: Chinese names and measures in English form: Liu Dacheng, Sun, Changshan, Baodong temple, and 'three hundred mu' — Chinese readings, or the Japanese readings (Ryū Daisei and so on) through which a 1916 Japanese reader met them?
open_questions.why_it_matters: Akutagawa's China is a Japan-mediated, bookish China, closer to a Liaozhai retelling than to reportage. Fully sinicised names make the English more 'authentic' than the Japanese feels; Japanese readings make it opaque. Either is defensible; mixing them is not.

open_questions.question: The third answer's equation — Liu is the worm, the worm is Liu — reads as Buddhist-flavoured paradox and as a plain statement of identity. Should the English keep its aphoristic snap, at the cost of sounding like a Zen epigram Akutagawa may be parodying along with the moralists?
open_questions.why_it_matters: It is the answer most readers remember, and the one most likely to be mistaken for the author's own verdict. Its tone decides whether the ending feels profound or deliberately over-neat.

body.reading:
Begin from the crux, because everything in the manner serves it. Part I is a held tableau: three men in killing heat, one of them naked, bound hand and foot with cord, lying on his back with an unglazed jar at his head, saying nothing, barely moving, like clay statues in a Guandi temple. The text withholds every reason for this and makes the reader wait in the heat with them. Part II supplies the reasons, slowly, through vanity and gossip rather than through any urgency of illness — Liu, it is made clear, did not feel ill and had never once been drunk. Part III narrows to a single body: sweat running into eyes that cannot be wiped, skin prickling as if pulled in all directions at once, thirst sharpened by the smell of wine from the jar, then the thing moving up the oesophagus, now like an earthworm, now like a gecko shifting its weight, now slipping out like a loach. Part IV jumps three years in a paragraph and turns a strange cure into destitution, then into a seminar. Keep those four movements distinct in English. Do not let the opening tableau acquire explanatory connectives it does not have, do not let the flashback hurry, do not let the expulsion scene be summarised, and do not let the last section slow into elegy.

The sound is learned and sensuous at once. The heat writing of Part I is dense with Sino-Japanese compounds and similes — roof tiles dully reflecting light like lead, cloud-peaks like hail roasted in an earthen pan, swallows' nests that might steam the chicks inside — and it returns in Part III as bodily sensation, so that the weather of the first page becomes the torture of the third. English that varies or thins this vocabulary breaks the link. Keep the repetitions that build it: heat, silence, stillness, the jar, the smell of wine growing minute by minute. The unglazed jar and Sun's white-feather fan are introduced as unidentified objects and identified later, in the narrator's own time; a translation that names their contents or owner early has rationalised the structure away. Dialogue, by contrast, is short and flat, the monk's especially, and should stay flat against the narrator's elaboration.

Names for the fluent failures to resist, in the house's terms: clarification — explaining what the wine worm is before or beyond the swimming thing in the jar, or glossing the monk's method as sympathetic magic; ennoblement — making the Chinese setting picturesquely exotic, or the ending wise; impoverishment — 'bug' or 'parasite' for a creature the text presents with mouth, eyes and an appetite; destroying the network of repeated words — varying wine, worm, drink, heat where the Japanese insists on them; and above all rationalisation of the close, where the three answers must remain a list the narrator declines to adjudicate, capped by his confession of ignorance and the dated sign-off, which should land as dryly in English as it does in Japanese. The monk's cure works exactly as promised and ruins the patient, and the text's position is that both halves of that sentence are simply true. Translate so that the reader, like the people of Changshan, is left repeating the question.
body.say: The reading above is complete. The three open questions are recommended to the editor as forks, with the first — how visibly to keep the scholarly pose — settled before drafting, since it determines register throughout.

voice_takes.label: Dry, exact, faintly antiquarian — a case history told deadpan, the grotesque left to do its own work.
Warmer and more novelistic — Liu's decline given pathos, the comedy broadened.
Flatter and more modern — shorter sentences, contemporary diction, the Chinese apparatus kept minimal.

revision.english: I

It is a heat unknown in recent years. Wherever one looks, the roof-tiles of the mud-plastered houses reflect the sunlight dully, like lead, so that even the swallows' nests hung beneath them seem, at this rate, like to steam the chicks and eggs within to death just as they are. What is more, every field that is a field, hemp or millet, hangs its head limply in the rising heat from the earth, and there is not one thing that, for all its greenness, is not wilted. The sky seen above those fields, too, whether from the warm vapours of these last days, the air near the ground, though clear, hangs thick and turbid, and here and there the piled clouds, like hail parched in an earthen pan, mere shapes, float in knobs. — The tale of the "wine worm" begins with three men who in this weather have gone out of their way to be upon a threshing-floor in the blazing sun.

Strangely, one of them lies stark naked on his back on the bare ground. What is more, for some reason or other, hand and foot he is wound round and round with thin cord. Yet the man himself shows no sign of suffering it as a hardship. He is short, of good colour, somehow giving a sense of dull heaviness, a man fat as a pig. Then a handy unglazed earthen jar is set at this man's pillow, but what is inside that, too, is not known.

Another is a monk of strikingly antique aspect, in a yellow robe with a small bronze ring hung from his ear. His skin is remarkably black in colour, and to judge from his curled hair and beard, he would seem to be a man come from somewhere west of the Congling Mountains. Until now he has been patiently flourishing a red-handled shubi to drive off the horseflies and flies that would settle upon the naked man, but he appears at last to have tired a little, and now he has come over beside the unglazed earthen jar and squats there portentously, in the attitude of a turkey.
notes: Congling: the Onion Ranges, the Pamirs; the text's vague learned geography for a westerner, kept as a name. shubi: a horsehair fly-whisk with religious and scholar-official use; kept here on first use and then as fly-whisk, as the fan and jar are planted as unexplained objects.

revision.english: The last stands far apart from these two, under the eaves of a thatched hut in the corner of the threshing-floor. This man grows only a perfunctory beard like a rat's tail on the tip of his chin, and wears a black cloth gown long enough to hide his heels, with a tea-brown sash whose knot hangs sloppily. To judge from the manner in which from time to time he preciously plies a fan made of white birds' feathers, he is most likely a Confucian scholar or something of the kind.
notes: Third man left as conjecture, as in the Japanese; his name, Sun Sensei, and the fan's ownership are not given until Part II, so not anticipated here.

revision.english: All three, as if by agreement, keep their mouths shut. What is more, they hardly so much as move, as though they took extraordinary interest in something now about to happen, and for that reason were all holding their breath.

It must be just noon. Whether because even the dogs are taking their midday nap, not a single bark is heard. The hemp and millet that enclose the threshing-floor shine their green leaves in the sun and rest hushed and utterly still. And the sky seen beyond them, stifling with heat over its whole face, trails heat-haze, so that even the piled clouds seem to be panting in this dry spell. Look where one will, the only things that seem to breathe are these three men. And those three keep silence like the clay images enshrined in a Guandi temple....
notes: Guandi temple kept without gloss: the simile is to the life-size clay figures set in such a temple, hence stock-still silence. Left for the margin rather than explained in line.

revision.english: Of course, this is no tale of Japan. — It is what happened one summer on the threshing-floor of a Liu at a place called Changshan in China.
II

The man lying naked in the blazing sun is the master of this threshing-floor, surnamed Liu, named Dacheng, one of the leading rich men of Changshan. This man's sole diversion is the drinking of wine, and from morning he has scarcely ever been known to part from the cup. And that, as the phrase has it, "Each time he drinks alone, he empties a whole jar" — a measure of wine beyond the common run of men. Though, as said before, "Fields by the walls, three hundred mu, half sown with millet," so there is not the least fear that his drinking should encumber his estate.
notes: Kept both set phrases as quotations and kept mu unconverted; jar renders the same vessel as the unglazed earthen jar at the pillow, to hold the link. "As said before" follows the source though the phrase has not occurred before in the text.

revision.english: Why it is that he lies naked in the blazing sun has a history behind it, and it is this. — That day Liu was together with Sun Sensei, his companion in drinking (this is the scholar who held the white-feather fan), in a well-aired room, leaning against a bamboo wife and fighting out a game on the board, when the maidservant, a yahuan, came and said, "A monk who says he is staying at the Hodoji temple or somewhere has just come, and says he must by all means see the master. What shall I do?"
notes: I keep Sun Sensei as printed with ruby, and yahuan on this first appearance with the gloss maidservant, then plain English after. Bamboo wife renders chikufujin, the hollow bamboo bolster leaned on in summer. Hodoji follows the Japanese ruby for the temple name; the maid's vagueness is kept as or somewhere.

revision.english: "What, the Hodoji?" So saying, Liu blinked his small eyes as if dazzled, then, raising his fat body that looked hot in itself, ordered, "Then show him in here." Then, with a glance at Sun Sensei's face, he added, "It will be that monk, I suppose."
notes: Liu says bozu here, not banso: I keep it as plain that monk against the narrator's standing barbarian monk, to hold the dismissive familiarity.

revision.english: The monk at the Hodoji temple is a barbarian monk come from the Western Regions. Since he both lends a hand at healing and practises the arts of the bedchamber, his fame stands high in these parts. Rumours all but miraculous are rife — that Zhang San's black cataract suddenly turned toward recovery, that Li Si's eunuch illness was healed on the spot, and the like. — Both men had heard these rumours. What business could have brought that barbarian monk now, taking the trouble to come all the way to Liu's? Liu, for his part, had no recollection whatever of having sent to fetch him.
notes: Zhang San and Li Si are stock rumour-names, left as pronounced. Black cataract renders kuro-naisho and eunuch illness renders byoen literally; I am unsure of the exact medical force in either case and have not smoothed them. Western Regions renders Seiiki.

revision.english: To note it in passing, Liu was not at all a man who delighted in visitors. But when he already had one visitor with him, and a new visitor came, he would generally receive him gladly. He had a childish vanity of the sort that might be described as showing off the fact of having a visitor before a visitor. Besides, today's barbarian monk was at this time the talk everywhere. He was by no means a visitor one would be ashamed to meet. — Liu's motives in saying he would meet him lay roughly here.
"What business can he have?"
notes: The text gives no speaker for p15-p16; left unattributed as in the source. Read as talk between Liu and Sun Sensei.

revision.english: "Alms-seeking, most likely. He will be asking for some charity, I suppose."
notes: The text gives no speaker for p15-p16; left unattributed as in the source.

revision.english: While the two were talking such things over between them, presently there entered, guided in by the yahuan, a monk of strange aspect, tall and with eyes like cut violet quartz. He wore a yellow robe, his grown-out curling hair hanging tiresomely over his shoulders. Still holding his red-handled shubi, he planted himself heavily in the middle of the room. He offered no greeting, nor did he speak.
notes: Kept yahuan for the young maidservant and shubi for the fly-whisk, as standing terms; sense is given by context.

revision.english: Liu hesitated for a while, but as that somehow grew unsettling to him, he ventured, "Have you some business with me?"
Whereupon the barbarian monk said, "You are the one, I take it, who is fond of wine."

"I am." The question was so abrupt that Liu, as he gave his vague answer, looked toward Sun Sensei as if seeking rescue. Sun Sensei, with a composed air, went on laying stones on the board by himself. He showed no disposition to take any part.
"You are afflicted with a rare disease. Are you aware of it?" the barbarian monk said, as if to make sure. Liu, hearing of a disease, made a dubious face, and, stroking his bamboo wife,
notes: Bamboo wife is a hollow bamboo bolster embraced in summer; the sentence runs on into p22.

revision.english: "A disease — you say?"
"It is."
"No, since I was a child..." As Liu was about to say something more, the barbarian monk cut him off.
"However much wine you drink, you never get drunk."
"..." Liu stared at the man's face and shut his mouth. In fact, however much wine this man drank, he had never once been drunk.

"That is the proof of the disease," the barbarian monk went on with a faint smile. "There is a wine worm in your belly. Unless it is removed, this disease will not be cured. I have come to cure your disease."
notes: I render the monk's self-word 貧道 as plain "I" to keep his speech flat and abrupt as the text gives it.

revision.english: "Can it be cured?" Liu cried out before he knew it, in an uncertain voice. And he was ashamed of himself for it.
"It can be cured, which is why I have come."
Then Sun Sensei, who had till now listened in silence to the exchange of questions and answers, suddenly put in a word.
"Will you use some medicine?"
"No, there is no need to use medicine or the like," the barbarian monk answered ungraciously.

Sun Sensei by nature despised the two teachings of the Daoists and the Buddhists almost without reason. Hence he had rarely ever spoken a word when in company with a Daoist priest or a Buddhist monk. That he had now taken a sudden fancy to intervene was wholly because his interest had been stirred by the words wine worm, for Sensei, who loved wine, hearing this, had grown a little uneasy lest there be a wine worm in his own belly as well. On hearing the barbarian monk's grudging answer, however, he suddenly felt as if he himself had been made a fool of, so with a slight grimace he began once more in silence to lay the pieces down as before. And at the same time he thought inwardly how foolish of his host Liu to receive such an arrogant monk.
Liu, for his part, of course paid no heed to any of this.
"Then will you use needles?"
notes: Text names no speaker. Taken as Liu to the monk, with p36-p38 continuing the same alternating question and answer.

revision.english: "No, it is a thing of still less trouble."
"Then is it a spell?"
"No, nor is it a spell."

After repeating such talk, the barbarian monk briefly explained the cure to them. — By his account, one had only to strip naked and keep still in the sun. To Liu this seemed a very easy matter. If so small a thing would cure him, there was nothing better than to be cured. And, though he was not aware of it, he was also a little moved by curiosity at undergoing the barbarian monk's treatment.

So at last Liu bowed his head of his own accord, and it came to this: "Then I must ask you to cure me, if you please." — Such is the reason why Liu lies naked upon the threshing-floor in the blazing sun.

Thereupon, saying he must not stir, the barbarian monk wound Liu's body round and round with thin cord. Then, bidding one of the servants, he had an unglazed earthen jar filled with wine brought to Liu's pillow. That Sun Sensei, the good friend of the wine-mound, should in the course of things have come to stand witness to this strange cure goes without saying.
notes: "good friend of the wine-mound" keeps the source phrase literal, as an ironic learned label for a drinking companion. Contents of the jar, wine, are given only here, when the narrator gives them.

revision.english: What sort of thing the wine worm is, what happens when it is no longer in the belly, and what the jar of wine at the pillow is for, no one knows but the barbarian monk alone. To put it so, Liu, who has gone out naked into the blazing sun knowing nothing, may seem very heedless, but what ordinary men do when they take a schooling and the like is in truth for the most part the same sort of thing.
notes: Kept the schooling comparison flat and cool as in the source, without sharpening into satire.

revision.english: III

It is hot. Sweat comes welling up with a prickle across the brow, and when it seems to have beaded it comes trickling, lukewarm, toward the eyes. As ill luck will have it, he is bound with thin cord, so of course there is no putting out a hand to wipe it. He tries moving his neck to turn the course of the sweat aside, but at that instant a violent dizziness seems ready to come on, so to his disappointment he gave up this plan too. All the while the sweat without ceremony wets the eyelids and, passing from the side of the nose round the mouth, runs on down beneath the chin. It is disagreeable beyond measure.

Until then he had lain with eyes open, staring hard at the sky seared white and the hemp-field with its drooping leaves, but once the sweat began to pour without restraint even that had to be given up. It was then that Liu learned for the first time that sweat stings when it gets into the eyes. And so, with the face of a sheep in the slaughterhouse, meekly shutting his eyes and lying still while the sun beats down upon him, now in turn the skin of the upper parts, face or body alike, began gradually to feel a certain pain. Over the whole surface of the skin a force is at work tending to move in every direction, while the skin itself has not the least elasticity against it. A pain that might best be described as a tingling everywhere — this is not the misery of prickly heat. Liu began to find it hateful that he had taken the barbarian monk's cure.

However, thinking it over afterwards, this was still the part that was less painful. — Before long his throat grows parched. Liu too knows the story of how Cao Mengde, or someone, cured the thirst of his soldiers by telling them there was a plum grove ahead. But now, picture as he will the sweet sourness of plums in his mind, his thirst is not a whit the less for it. He moves his jaw about, he bites his tongue, yet inside his mouth still keeps its heat. That too might still have been somewhat easier to bear, had there not been the unglazed earthen jar at his pillow. From the mouth of the jar the heavy smell of wine comes without break to assail his nose. And, though it may be fancy, he even feels that smell growing stronger with every minute. Thinking at least to look at the jar, Liu opened his eyes. Glancing upward, he sees the mouth of the jar and something like half of its amply bulging body. That alone is what he sees, but at the same time there rises before Liu's imagination the sight of wine the colour of gold brimming in the dim interior of that jar. Before he knew it he had licked his cracked lips with his dry tongue, yet there is no sign at all of saliva springing. Even the sweat, dried now by the sun, no longer flows as before.

Then a violent dizziness came, two or three times in succession. The headache has not abated since some time ago. In his heart Liu thought the barbarian monk ever more hateful. And he thought too why a man of his standing should have let such a fellow talk him round into suffering so foolish a torment. Meanwhile his throat grows ever more parched. His chest turns strangely queasy. He can no longer bear it, to lie still. So at last Liu resolved, and, panting, opened his mouth, meaning to ask the barbarian monk at his pillow to call off the cure. —
notes: "a man of his standing" for 自分ともあるもの: social standing, not a reflexive; he thinks one such as he should not have been talked round.

revision.english: At that very instant. Liu began to feel an indescribable lump creeping little by little from his chest up toward his throat. At one moment it seems to writhe like an earthworm, at another to edge along little by little like a gecko. In any case some soft thing, soft as it is, comes wriggling and pressing up the gullet. And at last, when it has forced its way past beneath the Adam's apple, all at once it slips slick out of the dark place like a loach or something and flies outward with force.
notes: Kept the three likenesses shifting — earthworm, gecko, loach — without fixing on one animal.

revision.english: And with that, from the quarter of the familiar unglazed earthen jar, there sounded a plop, as of something falling into wine.
Upon this the barbarian monk suddenly raised the haunches he had settled and began to undo the thin cord wound about Liu's body. The wine worm is out, so be at ease, is what he means.

"Has it come out?" Liu said as if groaning, lifting his swimming head, and out of sheer curiosity, forgetting even his thirst, crawled naked to the side of the jar. At this, Sun Sensei too, shading himself from the sun with his white-feather fan, came hurrying toward the two. When all three together peered into the jar, a thing like a small salamander, flesh-coloured as red clay, was swimming in the wine. In length perhaps three sun. It had a mouth, and it had eyes. As it swam it seemed somehow to be drinking the wine. At the sight of it Liu felt suddenly sick. ...
notes: Kept 'three sun' for length; a sun is about three centimetres. 'Red clay' renders shudei.

revision.english: IV

The effect of the barbarian monk's treatment appeared at once. From that day Liu Dacheng abruptly could drink no more wine. Now he will not bear even to smell it, they say. Strangely, from that time Liu's health began to fail little by little. This year is three years since he spat out the wine worm, and no trace remains of the round, fat figure of former years. Skin of poor lustre, greasy still, wraps the harsh bones of his face, and frost-touched hair at the temples lingers only faintly above the temples, and in a year none knows how many times he takes to his bed, they say.
notes: 'hair at the temples' renders sobin; 'above the temples' renders komekami. Kept the hearsay 'they say' for sou de aru.

revision.english: Yet it was not Liu's health alone that has failed since then. His estate too has declined headlong, and now of the walled fields counted at three hundred mu, most have passed into other hands. Liu himself, perforce, has taken the plough in unpractised hands and passes his days, day by day, in cheerlessness.
notes: 'walled fields counted at three hundred mu' keeps fukaku no den and mu from the set phrase quoted in p10; mu is a Chinese field measure.

revision.english: Since spitting out the wine worm, why has Liu's health failed? Why has the estate declined — if the spitting out of the wine worm and Liu's later destitution are set side by side in a relation of cause and effect, this is a question apt to occur to anyone. In fact this question has been repeated by people of every occupation living in Changshan, and from the mouths of those people answers of every kind have been given. The three answers set down here are in truth no more than the most representative chosen from among them.
First answer. The wine worm was Liu's fortune, and not Liu's disease. Through chancing to meet with a benighted barbarian monk, he willingly came to lose this heaven-given fortune.

Second answer. The wine worm was Liu's disease, and not Liu's fortune. For to drain a whole jar at a single drinking is quite beyond what an ordinary man can conceive. Had the wine worm not been removed, Liu must soon have died, without doubt. That being so, poverty and sickness arriving each in turn should rather be called happiness for Liu.

Third answer. The wine worm was neither Liu's disease nor Liu's fortune. Liu from of old drank nothing but wine. If wine is taken from Liu's life, afterwards nothing remains. That being so, Liu is the wine worm, the wine worm is Liu. Therefore Liu's parting with the wine worm is the same as killing himself. In short, from the day he could drink wine no more, Liu is Liu and yet is not Liu. If Liu himself was already gone, that the health and estate of the Liu of former days should have been lost is entirely natural, and a matter of course.
notes: Kept the identity sentence as plain aphorism, neither explaining its Buddhist colour nor smoothing it into paradox.

revision.english: Which of these answers comes nearest to the mark, I myself do not know. I have merely listed such moral judgments at the end of this tale, in imitation of the *Didacticism* of Chinese novelists.
notes: Kept Didacticism capitalised and in roman as printed, with italics to match the source emphasis; rendered both instances of 自分 as plain 'I / myself' with no inflation.

revision.english: — Fourth Month of the Fifth Year —
notes: Left the date literal and unresolved; the year is not determinable from the passage alone, so did not render as April 1916. Em dashes kept because the Japanese has them.

What sort of thing the wine worm is, what happens when it is no longer in the belly, and what the jar of wine at the pillow is for, no one knows but the barbarian monk alone. To put it so, Liu, who has gone out naked into the blazing sun knowing nothing, may seem very heedless, but what ordinary men do when they receive schooling and the like is in truth for the most part the same sort of thing.

Until then he had lain with eyes open, staring hard at the sky seared white and the hemp-field with its drooping leaves, but once the sweat began to pour without restraint even that had to be given up. It was then that Liu learned for the first time that sweat stings when it gets into the eyes. And so, with the face of a sheep in the slaughterhouse, meekly shutting his eyes and lying still while the sun beats down upon him, now in turn the skin of the upper parts, face or body alike, began gradually to feel a certain pain. Across every inch of skin something tugs in every direction at once, and the skin has no give in it at all. A pain that might best be described as a tingling everywhere. This is not the misery of prickly heat. Liu began to find it hateful that he had taken the barbarian monk's cure.

Yet it was not Liu's health alone that has failed since then. His estate too has declined headlong, and now of the fields by the walls counted as three hundred mu, most have passed into other hands. Liu himself, perforce, has taken the plough in unpractised hands and passes his days, day by day, in cheerlessness.

crux.for_the_english: Give the sensation in plain present-tense accumulation, not gothic description. The English should squirm, not shudder.
crux.point: A man is cured of the thing that made him himself, and the story will not say whether the cure saved or killed him.
crux.why: Liu Dacheng drinks a cask at a sitting and never gets drunk. A rude monk from the west says a wine worm lives in his belly, ties him naked in the noon heat of his own threshing-floor with a jar of wine at his pillow, and the worm, lured by the smell, crawls up his throat and drops into the jar — a three-inch, flesh-red, salamander-like thing with mouth and eyes, apparently drinking as it swims. From that day Liu cannot bear even the smell of wine. Within three years his health, then his three hundred mu of fields, then his whole former self are gone. Part IV then stops the story and lines up three answers — the worm was his fortune, not his disease; the worm was his disease, and poverty and sickness are still better than the death it would have brought; the worm was neither, because Liu was the worm and in losing it he killed himself — and the narrator says he does not know which is right, and that he has only listed them in imitation of the Didacticism of Chinese novelists. Every earlier pleasure of the tale, the heat, the grotesque cure, the comedy of the three waiting men, is retroactively put in question by that refusal. If the English lets any one answer win — by a sympathetic adjective for Liu, a sinister one for the monk, a wry or a mournful colouring in the final paragraphs — it has decided a case the text leaves open and become a fable about alcohol, or about quacks, or about genius destroyed by normality. None of those is this story.

crux.for_the_english: Keep the three answers parallel, evenly weighted and evenly plausible, in the same enumerating syntax. Keep the monk rude, abrupt and unexplained from first to last: he gives no greeting, answers Sun's questions ungraciously, states his diagnosis as fact. Do not make him a sage, a charlatan or a tempter. Keep Liu neither fool nor victim in the diction: he consents out of vanity, curiosity and a childish wish to show off a famous visitor, and the narrator reports those motives as coolly as he reports the weather.
crux.point: The narrator is a faux-scholarly intermediary, not a storyteller on the reader's side, and his asides are part of the mechanism.
crux.why: The tale is framed as a Chinese anecdote retold: it opens on the threshing-floor tableau with no explanation, breaks off to say of course this is not Japan but an incident at Changshan in China, flashes back with repeated deferrals ('the reason he lies there is this'), cross-refers to itself ('as said before'), quotes drinking and acreage in set Chinese phrases, digresses to compare Liu's ignorant submission to the treatment with ordinary people submitting to schooling, and signs off with a date. The erudition is real and also a pose; the citations and the numbered moral answers mimic a Chinese source the reader cannot check. That distance is what lets the impossible worm be reported like a case history.

payload.english: I

It is a heat unknown in recent years. Wherever one looks, the roof-tiles of the mud-plastered houses reflect the sunlight dully, like lead, so that even the swallows' nests hung beneath them seem, at this rate, like to steam the chicks and eggs within to death just as they are. What is more, every field that is a field, hemp or millet, hangs its head limply in the rising heat from the earth, and there is not one thing that, for all its greenness, is not wilted. The sky seen above those fields, too, whether from the warm vapours of these last days, the air near the ground, though clear, hangs thick and turbid, and here and there the piled clouds, like hail parched in an earthen pan, mere shapes, float in knobs. — The tale of the "wine worm" begins with three men who in this weather have gone out of their way to be upon a threshing-floor in the blazing sun.

Strangely, one of them lies stark naked on his back on the bare ground. What is more, for some reason or other, hand and foot he is wound round and round with thin cord. Yet the man himself shows no sign of suffering it as a hardship. He is short, of good colour, somehow giving a sense of dull heaviness, a man fat as a pig. Then a handy unglazed earthen jar is set at this man's pillow, but what is inside that, too, is not known.

His skin is remarkably black in colour, and to judge from his curled hair and beard, he would seem to be a man come from somewhere west of the Congling Mountains. Until now he has been patiently flourishing a red-handled shubi to drive off the horseflies and flies that would settle upon the naked man, but he appears at last to have tired a little, and now he has come over beside the unglazed earthen jar and squats there portentously, in the attitude of a turkey.

II

The man lying naked in the blazing sun is the master of this threshing-floor, surnamed Liu, named Dacheng, one of the leading rich men of Changshan. This man's sole diversion is the drinking of wine, and from morning he has scarcely ever been known to part from the cup. And that, as the phrase has it, "Each time he drinks alone, he empties a whole jar" — a measure of wine beyond the common run of men. Though, as said before, "Fields by the walls, three hundred mu, half sown with millet," so there is not the least fear that his drinking should encumber his estate.
notes: Kept both set phrases as quotations and kept mu unconverted; jar renders the same vessel as the unglazed earthen jar at the pillow, to hold the link. "As said before" follows the source though the phrase has not occurred before in the text.

payload.say: Drafted the summons and gossip passage without tipping the cure or the morals.

payload.english: Why it is that he lies naked in the blazing sun has a history behind it, and it is this. — That day Liu was together with Sun Sensei, his companion in drinking (this is the scholar who held the white-feather fan), in a well-aired room, leaning against a bamboo wife and fighting out a game on the board, when the maidservant, a yahuan, came and said, "A monk who says he is staying at the Hodoji temple or somewhere has just come, and says he must by all means see the master. What shall I do?"
notes: I keep Sun Sensei as printed with ruby, and yahuan on this first appearance with the gloss maidservant, then plain English after. Bamboo wife renders chikufujin, the hollow bamboo bolster leaned on in summer. Hodoji follows the Japanese ruby for the temple name; the maid's vagueness is kept as or somewhere.

payload.english: "What, the Hodoji?" So saying, Liu blinked his small eyes as if dazzled, then, raising his fat body that looked hot in itself, ordered, "Then show him in here." Then, with a glance at Sun Sensei's face, he added, "It will be that monk, I suppose."
notes: Liu says bozu here, not banso: I keep it as plain that monk against the narrator's standing barbarian monk, to hold the dismissive familiarity.

payload.english: The monk at the Hodoji temple is a barbarian monk come from the Western Regions. Since he both lends a hand at healing and practises the arts of the bedchamber, his fame stands high in these parts. Rumours all but miraculous are rife — that Zhang San's black cataract suddenly turned toward recovery, that Li Si's eunuch illness was healed on the spot, and the like. — Both men had heard these rumours. What business could have brought that barbarian monk now, taking the trouble to come all the way to Liu's? Liu, for his part, had no recollection whatever of having sent to fetch him.
notes: Zhang San and Li Si are stock rumour-names, left as pronounced. Black cataract renders kuro-naisho and eunuch illness renders byoen literally; I am unsure of the exact medical force in either case and have not smoothed them. Western Regions renders Seiiki.

payload.say: Drafted p14 to p21 in past-tense deadpan, keeping dialogue flat and terms of office unexplained.

payload.english: To note it in passing, Liu was not at all a man who delighted in visitors. But when he already had one visitor with him, and a new visitor came, he would generally receive him gladly. He had a childish vanity of the sort that might be described as showing off the fact of having a visitor before a visitor. Besides, today's barbarian monk was at this time the talk everywhere. He was by no means a visitor one would be ashamed to meet. — Liu's motives in saying he would meet him lay roughly here.
"What business can he have?"
notes: The text gives no speaker for p15-p16; left unattributed as in the source. Read as talk between Liu and Sun Sensei.

payload.english: "Alms-seeking, most likely. He will be asking for some charity, I suppose."
notes: The text gives no speaker for p15-p16; left unattributed as in the source.

payload.english: While the two were talking such things over between them, presently there entered, guided in by the yahuan, a monk of strange aspect, tall and with eyes like cut violet quartz. He wore a yellow robe, his grown-out curling hair hanging tiresomely over his shoulders. Still holding his red-handled shubi, he planted himself heavily in the middle of the room. He offered no greeting, nor did he speak.
notes: Kept yahuan for the young maidservant and shubi for the fly-whisk, as standing terms; sense is given by context.

payload.english: Liu hesitated for a while, but as that somehow grew unsettling to him, he ventured, "Have you some business with me?"
Whereupon the barbarian monk said, "You are the one, I take it, who is fond of wine."

"I am." The question was so abrupt that Liu, as he gave his vague answer, looked toward Sun Sensei as if seeking rescue. Sun Sensei, with a composed air, went on laying stones on the board by himself. He showed no disposition to take any part.
"You are afflicted with a rare disease. Are you aware of it?" the barbarian monk said, as if to make sure. Liu, hearing of a disease, made a dubious face, and, stroking his bamboo wife,
notes: Bamboo wife is a hollow bamboo bolster embraced in summer; the sentence runs on into p22.

payload.english: "A disease — you say?"
"It is."
"No, since I was a child..." As Liu was about to say something more, the barbarian monk cut him off.
"However much wine you drink, you never get drunk."
"..." Liu stared at the man's face and shut his mouth. In fact, however much wine this man drank, he had never once been drunk.

"That is the proof of the disease," the barbarian monk went on with a faint smile. "There is a wine worm in your belly. Unless it is removed, this disease will not be cured. I have come to cure your disease."
notes: I render the monk's self-word 貧道 as plain "I" to keep his speech flat and abrupt as the text gives it.

payload.english: "Can it be cured?" Liu cried out before he knew it, in an uncertain voice. And he was ashamed of himself for it.
"It can be cured, which is why I have come."
Then Sun Sensei, who had till now listened in silence to the exchange of questions and answers, suddenly put in a word.
"Will you use some medicine?"
"No, there is no need to use medicine or the like," the barbarian monk answered ungraciously.

Sun Sensei by nature despised the two teachings of the Daoists and the Buddhists almost without reason. Hence he had rarely ever spoken a word when in company with a Daoist priest or a Buddhist monk. That he had now taken a sudden fancy to intervene was wholly because his interest had been stirred by the words wine worm, for Sensei, who loved wine, hearing this, had grown a little uneasy lest there be a wine worm in his own belly as well. On hearing the barbarian monk's grudging answer, however, he suddenly felt as if he himself had been made a fool of, so with a slight grimace he began once more in silence to lay the pieces down as before. And at the same time he thought inwardly how foolish of his host Liu to receive such an arrogant monk.
Liu, for his part, of course paid no heed to any of this.
"Then will you use needles?"
notes: Text names no speaker. Taken as Liu to the monk, with p36-p38 continuing the same alternating question and answer.

payload.english: "No, it is a thing of still less trouble."
"Then is it a spell?"
"No, nor is it a spell."

After repeating such talk, the barbarian monk briefly explained the cure to them. — By his account, one had only to strip naked and keep still in the sun. To Liu this seemed a very easy matter. If so small a thing would cure him, there was nothing better than to be cured. And, though he was not aware of it, he was also a little moved by curiosity at undergoing the barbarian monk's treatment.

So at last Liu bowed his head of his own accord, and it came to this: "Then I must ask you to cure me, if you please." — Such is the reason why Liu lies naked upon the threshing-floor in the blazing sun.

Thereupon, saying he must not stir, the barbarian monk wound Liu's body round and round with thin cord. Then, bidding one of the servants, he had an unglazed earthen jar filled with wine brought to Liu's pillow. That Sun Sensei, the good friend of the wine-mound, should in the course of things have come to stand witness to this strange cure goes without saying.
notes: "good friend of the wine-mound" keeps the source phrase literal, as an ironic learned label for a drinking companion. Contents of the jar, wine, are given only here, when the narrator gives them.

payload.english: What sort of thing the wine worm is, what happens when it is no longer in the belly, and what the jar of wine at the pillow is for, no one knows but the barbarian monk alone. To put it so, Liu, who has gone out naked into the blazing sun knowing nothing, may seem very heedless, but what ordinary men do when they take a schooling and the like is in truth for the most part the same sort of thing.
notes: Kept the schooling comparison flat and cool as in the source, without sharpening into satire.

payload.say: Drafted the Part III opening sweat and skin-pain passage in present-tense sequence.

payload.english: III

It is hot. Sweat comes welling up with a prickle across the brow, and when it seems to have beaded it comes trickling, lukewarm, toward the eyes. As ill luck will have it, he is bound with thin cord, so of course there is no putting out a hand to wipe it. He tries moving his neck to turn the course of the sweat aside, but at that instant a violent dizziness seems ready to come on, so to his disappointment he gave up this plan too. All the while the sweat without ceremony wets the eyelids and, passing from the side of the nose round the mouth, runs on down beneath the chin. It is disagreeable beyond measure.

Until then he had lain with eyes open, staring hard at the sky seared white and the hemp-field with its drooping leaves, but once the sweat began to pour without restraint even that had to be given up. It was then that Liu learned for the first time that sweat stings when it gets into the eyes. And so, with the face of a sheep in the slaughterhouse, meekly shutting his eyes and lying still while the sun beats down upon him, now in turn the skin of the upper parts, face or body alike, began gradually to feel a certain pain. Over the whole surface of the skin a force is at work tending to move in every direction, while the skin itself has not the least elasticity against it. A pain that might best be described as a tingling everywhere — this is not the misery of prickly heat. Liu began to find it hateful that he had taken the barbarian monk's cure.

However, thinking it over afterwards, this was still the part that was less painful. — Before long his throat grows parched. Liu too knows the story of how Cao Mengde, or someone, cured the thirst of his soldiers by telling them there was a plum grove ahead. But now, picture as he will the sweet sourness of plums in his mind, his thirst is not a whit the less for it. He moves his jaw about, he bites his tongue, yet inside his mouth still keeps its heat. That too might still have been somewhat easier to bear, had there not been the unglazed earthen jar at his pillow. From the mouth of the jar the heavy smell of wine comes without break to assail his nose. And, though it may be fancy, he even feels that smell growing stronger with every minute. Thinking at least to look at the jar, Liu opened his eyes. Glancing upward, he sees the mouth of the jar and something like half of its amply bulging body. That alone is what he sees, but at the same time there rises before Liu's imagination the sight of wine the colour of gold brimming in the dim interior of that jar. Before he knew it he had licked his cracked lips with his dry tongue, yet there is no sign at all of saliva springing. Even the sweat, dried now by the sun, no longer flows as before.

payload.say: Drafted the expulsion in plain accumulating present for the body, past for the act.

payload.english: Then a violent dizziness came, two or three times in succession. The headache has not abated since some time ago. In his heart Liu thought the barbarian monk ever more hateful. And he thought too why a man of his standing should have let such a fellow talk him round into suffering so foolish a torment. Meanwhile his throat grows ever more parched. His chest turns strangely queasy. He can no longer bear it, to lie still. So at last Liu resolved, and, panting, opened his mouth, meaning to ask the barbarian monk at his pillow to call off the cure. —
notes: "a man of his standing" for 自分ともあるもの: social standing, not a reflexive; he thinks one such as he should not have been talked round.

payload.english: At that very instant. Liu began to feel an indescribable lump creeping little by little from his chest up toward his throat. At one moment it seems to writhe like an earthworm, at another to edge along little by little like a gecko. In any case some soft thing, soft as it is, comes wriggling and pressing up the gullet. And at last, when it has forced its way past beneath the Adam's apple, all at once it slips slick out of the dark place like a loach or something and flies outward with force.
notes: Kept the three likenesses shifting — earthworm, gecko, loach — without fixing on one animal.

payload.english: And with that, from the quarter of the familiar unglazed earthen jar, there sounded a plop, as of something falling into wine.
Upon this the barbarian monk suddenly raised the haunches he had settled and began to undo the thin cord wound about Liu's body. The wine worm is out, so be at ease, is what he means.

"Has it come out?" Liu said as if groaning, lifting his swimming head, and out of sheer curiosity, forgetting even his thirst, crawled naked to the side of the jar. At this, Sun Sensei too, shading himself from the sun with his white-feather fan, came hurrying toward the two. When all three together peered into the jar, a thing like a small salamander, flesh-coloured as red clay, was swimming in the wine. In length perhaps three sun. It had a mouth, and it had eyes. As it swam it seemed somehow to be drinking the wine. At the sight of it Liu felt suddenly sick. ...
notes: Kept 'three sun' for length; a sun is about three centimetres. 'Red clay' renders shudei.

payload.english: IV

The effect of the barbarian monk's treatment appeared at once. From that day Liu Dacheng abruptly could drink no more wine. Now he will not bear even to smell it, they say. Strangely, from that time Liu's health began to fail little by little. This year is three years since he spat out the wine worm, and no trace remains of the round, fat figure of former years. Skin of poor lustre, greasy still, wraps the harsh bones of his face, and frost-touched hair at the temples lingers only faintly above the temples, and in a year none knows how many times he takes to his bed, they say.
notes: 'hair at the temples' renders sobin; 'above the temples' renders komekami. Kept the hearsay 'they say' for sou de aru.

payload.english: Yet it was not Liu's health alone that has failed since then. His estate too has declined headlong, and now of the walled fields counted at three hundred mu, most have passed into other hands. Liu himself, perforce, has taken the plough in unpractised hands and passes his days, day by day, in cheerlessness.
notes: 'walled fields counted at three hundred mu' keeps fukaku no den and mu from the set phrase quoted in p10; mu is a Chinese field measure.

payload.english: Since spitting out the wine worm, why has Liu's health failed? Why has the estate declined — if the spitting out of the wine worm and Liu's later destitution are set side by side in a relation of cause and effect, this is a question apt to occur to anyone. In fact this question has been repeated by people of every occupation living in Changshan, and from the mouths of those people answers of every kind have been given. The three answers set down here are in truth no more than the most representative chosen from among them.
First answer. The wine worm was Liu's fortune, and not Liu's disease. Through chancing to meet with a benighted barbarian monk, he willingly came to lose this heaven-given fortune.

Second answer. The wine worm was Liu's disease, and not Liu's fortune. For to drain a whole jar at a single drinking is quite beyond what an ordinary man can conceive. Had the wine worm not been removed, Liu must soon have died, without doubt. That being so, poverty and sickness arriving each in turn should rather be called happiness for Liu.

Third answer. The wine worm was neither Liu's disease nor Liu's fortune. Liu from of old drank nothing but wine. If wine is taken from Liu's life, afterwards nothing remains. That being so, Liu is the wine worm, the wine worm is Liu. Therefore Liu's parting with the wine worm is the same as killing himself. In short, from the day he could drink wine no more, Liu is Liu and yet is not Liu. If Liu himself was already gone, that the health and estate of the Liu of former days should have been lost is entirely natural, and a matter of course.
notes: Kept the identity sentence as plain aphorism, neither explaining its Buddhist colour nor smoothing it into paradox.

payload.english: Which of these answers comes nearest to the mark, I myself do not know. I have merely listed such moral judgments at the end of this tale, in imitation of the *Didacticism* of Chinese novelists.
notes: Kept Didacticism capitalised and in roman as printed, with italics to match the source emphasis; rendered both instances of 自分 as plain 'I / myself' with no inflation.

payload.english: — Fourth Month of the Fifth Year —
notes: Left the date literal and unresolved; the year is not determinable from the passage alone, so did not render as April 1916. Em dashes kept because the Japanese has them.

chapter_summaries.0: Part I. Blazing heat over tiled roofs, fields, cloud-peaks. Three men on Liu threshing-floor at noon: one naked, bound hand and foot, with unglazed jar at pillow; one dark-skinned western monk in yellow robe with fly-whisk; one long-gowned man with white-feather fan under eaves. All silent, barely moving, like clay statues in a Guandi temple. Narrator adds: not Japan but Changshan, China.

hard_spots.why_hard: 「独酌する毎に輒、一甕を尽す」 and 「負郭の田三百畝、半は黍を種う」 are quoted as proof-texts for prodigious drinking and wealth. Need to keep as quotations, not naturalise, and keep mu as mu with note; rendering jar/cask must match the jar at the pillow.
comparison of Liu's ignorant submission to schooling is cool authorial irony, not compassion; ennobling it into satire on education or softening it misplaces tone.
Cao Mengde's plum grove to cure thirst; Liu tries the trick and it fails. Needs minimal note only; context already gives sense.

expulsion similes shift earthworm / gecko / loach, then jar animal: flesh-red like red clay, like small salamander, three sun long, with mouth and eyes, apparently drinking as it swims. Must not reduce to bug or parasite and must keep shifting likeness, not fix one animal.

three answers must stay evenly weighted and aphoristic, especially third: Liu is the worm, the worm is Liu. Buddhist colour and plain identity at once; must not sound like quoted Zen wisdom nor like explanation.

narrator confesses ignorance and says he imitates the Didacticism of Chinese novelists, capital D in source, then signs 五年四月. Keep capitalised foreign word and dry sign-off; do not turn into wise closure. Date is ambiguous year-month; annotate, do not resolve.

part_summaries.summary: Part I. Blazing heat over tiled roofs, fields, cloud-peaks. Three men on Liu threshing-floor at noon: one naked, bound hand and foot, with unglazed jar at pillow; one dark-skinned western monk in yellow robe with fly-whisk; one long-gowned man with white-feather fan under eaves. All silent, barely moving, like clay statues in a Guandi temple. Narrator adds: not Japan but Changshan, China.

Part II. The naked man is owner Liu Dacheng, rich in 300 mu, who drinks a jar at a sitting and never gets drunk. Playing chess with drinking friend Sun Sensei, he admits the famed western monk from Hodoji temple. Monk without greeting diagnoses a wine worm in belly as cause of never drunkenness and offers cure by lying naked still in sun. Sun asks once about drugs, is rebuffed, falls silent. Liu consents from ease, curiosity and vanity; is bound with cord, jar of wine set at pillow, Sun stays to watch.

Part III. Liu alone in heat: sweat into eyes he cannot wipe, dizziness, skin prickling as if pulled all ways, raging thirst sharpened by unbroken smell of wine from jar, headache. As he opens mouth to stop cure, a soft mass crawls up gullet like earthworm, like gecko, slips out like loach with a plop into jar. Monk unties him: worm is out. All three peer in: flesh-red like red clay, like small salamander about three sun long, with mouth and eyes, seemingly drinking as it swims. Liu feels sick.

Part IV. Cure works at once: Liu cannot drink, cannot bear smell. In three years health fails, former fat figure gone, often bedridden; 300 mu mostly lost, he ploughs himself. Narrator poses why health and estate failed and lists three representative answers from Changshan people: worm was fortune lost through folly; worm was disease and poverty is better than death; worm was neither because Liu was the worm. Declares he does not know which is right, has only listed them in imitation of Chinese novelists' Didacticism. Signs Fifth year, fourth month.

bible.say: Cure works and ruins; text refuses to choose among fortune, disease, or identity readings. Keep tableau unexplained, monk rude and unexplained, dialogue flat against elaborate heat-writing, worm concrete with mouth and eyes, three answers parallel and declined, sign-off dry.

style_sheet.annotation_density: sparse; note only what sentence cannot give: mu, sun, Baodong/Hodoji temple name form, Cao Mengde plum-grove trick, Guandi temple statues, Didacticism capitalisation. Never gloss worm, method, or morals.
style_sheet.author_voice: learned and sensuous at once: dense Sino-Japanese heat similes and bodily accumulation in plain sequence, short flat dialogue, dry ironic asides and self-references. English should squirm in Part III, not shudder in gothic; should enumerate in Part IV, not elegise.
style_sheet.honorifics_and_names: Chinese pinyin for Chinese places and persons to keep not-Japan frame explicit: Liu Dacheng, Changshan, Zhang San, Li Si, Cao Mengde; temple as Hodoji (Baodong) with note on Japanese reading versus Chinese Baochuang. Keep Sun Sensei with Sensei, not Master Sun or Mr Sun, because text prints 孫先生 with Japanese ruby and Japanese mediation is part of pose; narrator's 自分 as I with no honorific inflation.
style_sheet.keep_in_japanese: keep Didacticism exactly capitalised as in source; keep mu for 田 measure and sun for worm length with note; keep shubi, yahuan, Guandi on first use with gloss if needed, then plain English; do not keep ordinary words in Japanese.
style_sheet.quotation: Japanese 「」 and 『』 to English double quotes; keep quoted set Chinese phrases as quotations to show pose of citation.
style_sheet.register: slightly formal, faintly archaic learned English for narration; plain contemporary for dialogue, especially monk's bluntness. No picturesque exoticism, no modern slang, no moralising adjectives that favour one answer.
style_sheet.ruby_and_italics: no ruby in English; do not reproduce glosses like つばめ except in notes if needed. Italics only for romanised terms kept in Japanese and for the printed English word Didacticism, matching source emphasis.

release.colophon:
底本：「芥川龍之介全集　第一巻」岩波書店
　　　1995（平成7）年11月8日発行
親本：「鼻」春陽堂
　　　1918（大正7）年7月8日発行
入力：earthian
校正：林めぐみ
1998年11月13日公開
2004年3月9日修正
青空文庫作成ファイル：
このファイルは、インターネットの図書館、青空文庫（http://www.aozora.gr.jp/）で作られました。入力、校正、制作にあたったのは、ボランティアの皆さんです。

crux.for_the_english: Give the sensation in plain present-tense accumulation, not gothic description. The English should squirm, not shudder.
crux.point: A man is cured of the thing that made him himself, and the story will not say whether the cure saved or killed him.
crux.why: Liu Dacheng drinks a cask at a sitting and never gets drunk. A rude monk from the west says a wine worm lives in his belly, ties him naked in the noon heat of his own threshing-floor with a jar of wine at his pillow, and the worm, lured by the smell, crawls up his throat and drops into the jar — a three-inch, flesh-red, salamander-like thing with mouth and eyes, apparently drinking as it swims. From that day Liu cannot bear even the smell of wine. Within three years his health, then his three hundred mu of fields, then his whole former self are gone.
